However, the basic transformer model lacks a clear mechanism for allocating attention weights, which are inherently dependent on previous computations.  To address this limitation, an alternative approach modifies the attention mechanism to yield adaptive attention weights tied to specific context vectors, which facilitates easier incorporation of context information.  In this paper, we go a step further by deriving a closed-form solution for attention weights, thus enabling optimized context-adaptive attention without relying on costly training processes.  Our proposed context-adaptive attention mechanism is highly versatile and can be applied across multiple context vectors.  We experimentally validate its effectiveness on three tasks, including bidirectional machine translation, universal machine translation, and summarization, which demonstrate significant improvements in performance.  Our code is openly available on GitHub and the Clam format used in training is openly released on Cloud Carrier.  With further optimization, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on WMT 2014 English-to-German translation, outperforming previous best results by a 0.48% improvement in BLEU score.  A brief discussion on analyzing attention weights through context vectors and a consideration of replacing the general heuristic point-wise product with a learned general context vector is also provided.  All our models are trained using the Clam format, which is an open format, and the source code is available on GitHub.  With further optimization, our method achieves a state-of-the-art result of 29.19 BLEU score on WMT 2014 English-to-German translation.  An extended version of this work has been published in a concurrent research by Pham et al.  Although our work was initially submitted in September 2018, the experiments and models were generated later, which led to the observed performance gains.  Our proposed method simplifies the attention mechanism through an invariant property, as a consequence of which, it facilitates easier incorporation of context information.  In contrast, the concurrent research complicates the attention mechanism to achieve the same effect.  In addition, our model exhibits the capability of allocating adaptive attention weights tied to specific context vectors with minimal computational overhead.  As an example, to achieve the same performance on the ensemble model of WMT 2014 English-to-German translation with 29.19 BLEU score, the concurrent research requires over 20 GB of memory and 50 seconds per sequence on a V100 GPU, as against 5 GB and 0.1 seconds per sequence on the same GPU, for the same translation task.

This paper defines a set of degree $K$ simple elementary subalgebras, denoted as $\mathscr{P}(\mathfrak{g}, K)$, which generate a Lie algebra of nilpotency class $K$. \cal O}1$ GeV scale threshold experiments like HKS and FQS and future experiments like the Poulter and the next generation of HIF are primarily limited by their limiting radii, which are currently constrained by our understanding of nuclear force short-range behavior as modeled in potentials like the Nijmegen and Bonn ones. The impact of these potentials on the smallest non-zero momentum transfer values as a function of radius has not been thoroughly analyzed before. In this study, we examine how different force models affect momentum transfer values at the smallest non-zero momentum transfer values as a function of radius and the associated two-body scattering length, which is an important factor in determining the four-body ground state energy for systems like diprotons. We found that the two-body scattering length is highly sensitive to the range of the forces and requires more precise determination than previously accounted for, especially when considering the effects of meson exchanges above the nucleon resonance scale. As a result, experiments with a sensitivity of ${\cal O}1$ GeV will not have a significant issue in determining this quantity accurately and reliably. Nevertheless, to address concerns about four-body force effects, we found that the ground state energy of four-nucleon systems is insensitive to the range of the nuclear force at the level of ${\cal O}1$ GeV, thus making experiments with higher precision necessary to detect possible non-standard four-nucleon interactions.  Furthermore, we discovered that the volume where the ground state energy of four-nucleon systems converges to the actual value is quite large, at approximately 100 fm$^3$, which is an important finding that will be useful for interpreting future data from high precision few-nucleon experiments and threshold experiments with few-nucleon final states.

Secondly, implementing decorrelated trials poses a methodological hurdle. To address these obstacles, we propose an innovative approach where we set a maximum acceptable density discrepancy threshold. By doing so, we can simultaneously increase the number of unitary parameters and guarantee density accuracy, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. Additionally, our method enables decorrelation of trial states with minimal computational expense, leading to significant energetic gains. Our findings, published in the current study, demonstrate that this approach is universally applicable across different types of unitary parameters and common ab initio models. Specifically, we observed a 5-7 times reduction in computational time per unitary rotation, along with improved energetic convergence, especially when trials are decorrelated. This method holds particular significance for future multi-electron quantum simulations using NNs.

Many current approaches for estimating global model-agnostic feature importance are, however, highly prone to distortion by correlated variables, which can lead to unreliable results.  Our research tackles this challenge by introducing a new family of global model-agnostic feature importance measures that not only account for the dependence among variables but also provide consistent results across multiple related data sets.  We further develop an efficient computational method for calculating these importance values and demonstrate their effectiveness in multiple real-world scenarios.  Our results show that our new importance measures outperform state-of-the-art approaches known for their robustness, according to multiple reliability metrics.  We also find that our methods provide results that are as intuitive as those produced by model-dependent feature importance measures, such as SHAP.  Our research provides a new framework for assessing feature importance in a way that is both data-set independent and robust to correlation issues.  We make our code available for public use.  Our research also highlights the challenge of reliably evaluating feature importance in complex, real-world scenarios with many variables and a large number of data sets.  We propose a set of metrics and procedures that can help others to consistently and robustly compare the performance of different feature importance measures.  We apply these metrics and procedures to evaluate multiple approaches for calculating global model-agnostic feature importance, including our new family of importance values.  We make our evaluation code publicly available for use by others. We introduce a novel framework, labeled source data can be toxic, which addresses a common assumption in existing UDA research. Our proposed framework consists of three scenarios: (1) removes all labeled data from the source, (2) utilizes a limited set of labeled source samples, and (3) makes no reference to the source labels. We develop a new method, an adaptive graph mixture model (AGMM), which addresses the last scenario. AGMM involves three primary components: (1) a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) that models the distribution of data within each domain and adapts to the target domain, (2) an adaptive threshold determinant that determines the domain identity of target samples based on their mixture probabilities, and (3) a performance-driven filter that removes target samples not deemed relevant by the adaptive threshold. We conduct extensive experiments with three UDA scenarios, including a novel study on zero-shot UDA, using the recently released LSO dataset. Additionally, we analyze the performance of various domain adaptation methods in comparison to our proposed AGMM approach. Our results demonstrate that AGMM outperforms existing methods by a significant margin in all evaluated domains, with performance gains of up to 24.8% according to the MSN score. Furthermore, we observe that deep learning-based methods struggle with domain adaptation when left unchecked, as illustrated in the accompanying video. Our study also yields key findings: (1) the overfitting issue in deep UDA has been overstated, (2) the widespread use of evaluation protocols that do not account for zero-shot UDA poses a significant problem, and (3) a universally accepted benchmark for zero-shot UDA remains to be established. Inspired by these outcomes, we launch the LSO dataset and associated evaluation protocols for zero-shot and extensive UDA studies. Moreover, we publicly release the code and models for all experiments conducted in this research.

The detection method involves identifying the magnetospheric radiation field that arises from the accelerating shock front. The detection time can be minimized by launching space-based missions, such as the GRBM (Gamma-Ray Burst Monitor) mission, which can detect these shocks within $T_{90} \approx 5.8$ days. The detection of GRB 190819B, which exhibited an unusual X-ray tail, is analyzed in the context of this framework. This analysis suggests that the X-ray tail could be magnetospheric radiation arising from the shock front, specifically the frozen-in plasma of the shock front interacting with the host galaxy's magnetic field. However, other external magnetic fields like the magnetospheric field of the host galaxy or a gamma-ray burst magnetosphere can also contribute to such X-ray tails. Our approach utilizes model checking techniques to create standardized safety protocols that account for potential hazards in a system's design.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we applied it to a case study of an aircraft's fly-by-wire system, utilizing the VHS safety standard framework.  However, our method is versatile and can be adapted to comply with a wide range of safety standards, such as IEC 61508, ISO 26262, or EN 50128, among others.  The system development process can be broken down into two primary phases:  design and verification.  During the design phase, system architects outline the system's architecture, define its performance requirements, and designate safety-relevant components.  In the verification phase, where our method is employed, designers perform a series of safety-related checks using model checking techniques to create and apply safety protocols to prevent hazards in the system's design.  To effectively integrate our method into the system development process, we established a safety-protocol framework called SafProt, which facilitates the creation and management of safety protocols through a set of safety-relevant markers.  By utilizing SafProt, we can adapt a wide range of safety standards to comply with the IEEE AADL specification.  To further enhance the development process, we recommend incorporating our method into an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) through a Safety Plug-in, which we call SafPlug.  To verify the efficacy of our approach, we applied it to the aircraft's fly-by-wire system case study, utilizing SafProt and SafPlug.  The results showed that our method successfully created safety protocols for preventing hazards in the system's design, and with SafPlug, we were able to reduce the time and effort required to verify the system's safety by approximately three times.  Ultimately, our method offers a versatile solution for creating functional safety standards in complex systems development, as demonstrated by the aircraft's fly-by-wire system case study. A new finding reported here indicates that D-alpha line emission during plasma shutdowns originates from regions where the plasma temperature is around $0.5\; \text{keV}$. It has also been observed that plasma temperature affects D-alpha emission, showing an increase during shutdowns when the plasma interface with the wall is cooler. This effect varies with plasma temperature and can be described by a fractional D-charge e-folding length of around $0.35$ times the major radius of the MST tokamak. It is suggested that D-alpha line emission during plasma shutdowns is caused by interface instability leading to exponential D-charge depletion, and accompanied by the formation of a plasma sheath and electron filaments observed in other tokamak plasma scenarios. Furthermore, this D-alpha emission phenomenon is found to occur even when a plasma shutdown is triggered by an internal MHD event, and it is proposed that D-alpha emission during plasma shutdowns provides a diagnostic tool to study the dynamics of plasma near the wall, and could also be affected by other plasma states, and may serve as an indicator of the plasma boundary condition for future long-pulse discharges in magnetic confinement devices. 

  It is worth noting that D-alpha emission during plasma shutdowns provides a diagnostic of the plasma boundary, and it is essential to understand this phenomenon to operate magnetic confinement devices successfully.

This study examines a chain of interacting atoms that are linked by a classical reservoir with correlated noise, using application of the quantum semi-classical approximation. We find that interacting atoms cannot reach a non-equilibrium steady state when driven by uncorrelated noise, but demonstrate that a steady state can be achieved with correlated noise, specifically when the correlation disappears at high frequencies. This phenomenon is attributed to the presence of a quantum phase transition driven by the interaction strength. Additionally, the steady state displays a unique thermodynamic characteristic that differs significantly from that of isolated systems, specifically in relation to a particular entropy quantity known as quasi-entropy. We further investigate these findings by considering specific types of correlated noise, such as laser drives and spontaneous emissions from multiple locations, as well as examining how they impact the steady state, particularly when there is a transition between a steady state that is entangled and one that is separable. Lastly, this study demonstrates that a steady state that is entangled can be achieved with uncorrelated noise by utilizing a particular type of noise at one location, specifically an amplitude-damping drive. This research provides multiple avenues for experimental verification of these novel non-equilibrium driving scenarios. Additionally, it highlights the complexity of driven quantum systems that are linked to a classical environment with correlated noise, specifically in relation to systems that exhibit a transition between a steady state that is entangled and one that is separable, as this situation is more common than previously anticipated. Furthermore, this study stresses the importance of carefully selecting both the type and location of driving locations when utilizing multi-location driving setups, specifically in relation to the creation of entangled steady states, as this may have broader implications for areas such as quantum communication.

. special case of a classical geometric scenario - the case of a surface with a prescribed curvature profile, a concept initially explored by Cercignani and Sernas in 1975. This surface model is applied to study the asymptotic behavior of a surface undergoing a simple shear flow in an environment where the ambient fluid follows a Boltzmann distribution. As time passes, the surface reaches a stationary state described by a modified curvature equation, which takes into account boundary conditions and is solved analytically for this specific surface model, resulting in a novel fractional curvature equation. Additionally, we demonstrate that this surface model exhibits a fractional memory effect, which decays over time in a power-law manner dependent on the Knudsen number. This is further confirmed by numerical simulations. Our analysis shows that for small Knudsen numbers, the surface model approaches a traditional memory effect, while for larger Knudsen numbers, the model displays a power-law memory effect, a phenomenon observed previously in a related surface model. A key finding in this paper is that this power-law memory effect is uniquely associated with a specific simple shear flow scenario. This is demonstrated by numerically solving the modified curvature equation for a step change in pressure, where the surface model exhibits a power-law memory effect for a small Knudsen number of 0.1, but transitions to a non-power-law memory effect for a larger Knudsen number of 10. This behavior is a distinct surface model phenomenon, rather than a general fractional diffusion coefficient effect. A new, a priori derived fractional curvature model is also examined and compared to these results, which highlights the differences and limitations of fractional models in this specific surface model context. This research offers a unique perspective on the memory effect in a surface model, which has implications for the validity of fractional models in this scenario. As a result, this study may contribute to a reevaluation of the application of fractional models in similar surface models. Although the memory effect in these models is power-law dependent on the Knudsen number, which accurately captures the asymptotic behavior for large Knudsen numbers, a more detailed analysis is needed to address the validity of these models for small Knudsen numbers. This research may also be of interest in tackling the valid range of applicability of a modified curvature equation in a surface model, which is a critical aspect in the correct modeling of microscale surface processes. As a consequence of this analysis, a new research direction is opened up, which focuses on the asymptotic behavior of a simple shear flow surface model,

This study evaluates the parton distribution function uncertainty for the LHC's $pp$ data and finds it to be significantly lower at 0.04%. The LHC's better performance can be attributed to more precise measurements of the $W$ and $Z$ boson rapidity distributions, particularly in the electron and muon channels with better resolution, where uncertainties are reduced by half when compared to the D0's Tevatron measurements. Furthermore, this study assesses the parton distribution function uncertainty for the future colliders such as the FCC-ee and ILC, but finds it to be dominated by other experimental uncertainties which are currently too high to be overwhelmed by parton distribution function uncertainties. Additionally, this study evaluates the parton distribution function uncertainty for the $Z$ boson mass measurement at the LHC and finds it to be identical to that of the $W$ boson due to similar production processes and experimental uncertainties. As a result, the combined uncertainty for the $Z$ boson mass measurement at the LHC is also expected to be as low as 0.04%. The LHC's $pp$ data and future experiments' capabilities to minimize parton distribution function uncertainties can lead to precision $W$ and $Z$ boson mass measurements, making them ideal for monitoring the evolution of QCD and ensuring the accuracy of parton distribution functions. As a consequence of improved precision, we also analyze the sensitivity of the $W$ and $Z$ boson mass measurements to the strong coupling constant. As a result, the sensitivity to the strong coupling constant for the LHC's $pp$ data and future experiments is dominated by the beam flux and is characterized by the total luminosity times the momentum transfer, which primarily originates from the $Z$ boson production process as a vector boson scattering process. have emerged as a key area of study in machine learning and graph theory, with applications across multiple domains including recommender systems, drug design, and fault diagnosis.  However, the effectiveness of GNN models can be compromised when graph datasets exhibit a rare yet common phenomenon known as node isolation.  Node isolation occurs when a node on the graph is unable to exchange information with any other node, largely due to poorly designed training protocols.  In reality, many real-world graphs are highly disconnected and contain isolated nodes, which can lead to devastatingly poor performance when using GNNs for node classification.  This research proposes a new type of GNN called the Multi-Layer Local Mix (MLLM) module, which can enhance the performance of existing GNNs by an average of 41% according to our experiments, while also successfully addressing the node isolation issue.  The MLLM module exploits the structural hierarchy within graphs by locally exchanging information at different graph layers, and selectively aggregates the learned representations from each layer based on the layer's connection status.  We further validate our approach by applying the MLLM module to three popular GNN models, which can improve the state-of-the-art performance on many datasets, and also provide a readable implementation of our work. Our study introduces an alternative, where the interaction field is composed of many dark particles with a certain velocity distribution.  Using numerical simulations, we investigated how these "dust" interactions affect galaxy evolution.  Our results show that a small fraction of interacting particles is sufficient to significantly alter the behavior of baryons, yet the distribution of these particles must conform to a specific pattern to adequately model the effects of dark matter-baryon interactions.  Our findings also indicate that a system of interacting particles can mimic the behavior of a single scalar field up to certain resolutions, but displays greater variability at higher resolutions. our Sun, is influenced by a complex interplay of magnetic field generation, evolution, and interaction.  This interplay affects the development of magnetic field-induced features like patters, loops, and dots, which are all observed in the images from the William Herschel Observatory's SPIRIT II camera.  By analyzing these features, recent findings have uncovered various astronomical phenomena, including the detection of a highly active, cycling star similar to our Sun, as well as evidence suggesting that some stars experience a significant increase in activity near the equator, which may be indicative of a'solar-like' differential rotation phenomenon.  Furthermore, observations have revealed numerous loops and arcades, which are likely the footprints of X-ray flares, as well as a vast population of tiny features, which are likely the results of numerous small flares and rotations of magnetic patches. approach against adversarial attacks, dubbed 'Adversarial Trajectory Analysis.' It generates a set of simplified, 2D trajectories around which an adaptive boundary is created to contain and redirect malicious 3D approaches. The defense is adaptable to various starting points and directions, and its effectiveness is shown across diverse adversarial techniques including PGD, FGSM, and CW attacks. Empirical results indicate that this method achieves a notable balance between accuracy restoration and attack containment, with minimal computational overhead. It is worth noting that while this defense method is presented in the context of 3D CNNs, its concepts can be applied to adversarial robustness assessments across various model types and dimensions. The code is openly available on GitHub for replication purposes.  In the process, we highlight the shortcomings of existing evaluation metrics and propose novel performance indicators, including Adversarial Containment Ratio and Restoration Accuracy Threshold. These proposed metrics demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in effectively containing and redirecting malicious inputs while also successfully restoring original model accuracy. Furthermore, our study emphasizes the importance of comprehensive evaluation strategies that address the inherent time and data biases associated with adversarial testing data. Based on our findings, we suggest best practices for future research focused on comparing and evaluating adversarial defense methods. The code is openly available on GitHub for replication purposes.  We present a novel, low-latency video compression technique called Field-Crossing Compression, and investigate its image coding components for reducing redundancy. A proposed algorithm, named FC-SR, is introduced, and outperforms existing strategies by achieving up to 5% better PSNR quality, and 3% better SSIM score, while requiring no extra bits. Our approach also exhibits superior visual clarity, as shown in the included videos and images. The code is openly available on GitHub for replication purposes.  We demonstrate that pre-trained Backbones, specifically those based on multi-scale attention and adaptive average aggregation, are susceptible to malicious input attacks, particularly in low-bitrate scenarios. An alternative, named Multi-Path Attention Aggregate (MA^2), is presented as a robust solution, as it is inherently immune to such attacks due to its adaptive pooling mechanisms. Our proposed approach achieves comparable compression quality (PSNR/SSIM) to existing methods, specifically the widely-used MobileNet-V2, while ensuring the integrity of compressed images upon decoding. The code is openly available on GitHub for replication purposes. If $\Omega$ is a component of the set where the modulus of $f$ is less than $1$, bound by the curve defined by $\{|z-w|^2 < 1/(|f(z)|^2)\}$, then we demonstrate that $\Omega$ is simply connected. Additionally, if $f(z)$ has a maximum modulus of less than $1$, then we prove that $\Omega$ is an Euclidean disk. These results extend previous work by Averbach and Gallardo to include the case of infinite boundaries. Similarly, they complement the Poincare-Belletty Theorem for the case of finite boundaries. Our method introduces the concept of a new integral invariant measure across the boundary of U. If the boundary of U has non-zero measure, then this new integral can vary while $f$ remains constant. Conversely, if the variation of the new integral is zero for all choices of $\Omega$, then $f$ is constant. If the boundary of U is not simply connected, then we show that there are multiple possible definitions for this new integral. Subsequently, if the variation of the new integral is zero for all choices of $\Omega$, then $f$ is a boundary point multiplying function, i.e. there exists a function $g$ on the boundary of U such that $f(z) = g(z) / (1 - \langle z, w \rangle^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}$ for some $w$ in the interior of the unit disk, and it is shown that this condition is both necessary and sufficient. These results have implications for the Ahlfors conformal distance distance measure and the Chern-Simons flow on bounded planar domains. Lastly, we provide a new definition for the Schiffer variation that applies to all bounded planar domains, and demonstrate that this new definition is equivalent to the original definition due to Schiffer, provided the domain is an Euclidean disk. Subsequently, we show that the original Schiffer variation fails to define a path-independent measure across the boundary of some bounded planar domains, and provide a new variational formula for the Chern-Simons flow on bounded planar domains. This new formula provides a new definition for the Schiffer variation, and it is demonstrated that this new definition is both necessary and sufficient to ensure the path independence of the original Schiffer variation. RFDNet, the proposed model, leverages a recursive feature learning approach to produce optimal features for matching.  It initializes with a basic feature extraction network, Branch1, before entering an iterative enhancement loop consisting of multiple branch modules.  Each iteration represents a separate matching task with its own network, systematically integrating output from the previous iteration and the original image, using both a fusion module and a revision module.  The iterative process allows the model to adapt feature extraction according to matching objectives, ultimately producing reliable matches for extensive dense image matching scenarios.  Experimental results show the model achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods on multiple datasets, with ease of implementation and computational efficiency making it a suitable solution for real-world applications.  Furthermore, the model's general feature learning ability is demonstrated through successful application to scene classification and border-forecasting tasks, with code publicly available for use. selecting the most effective samples from a large pool of choices, with the goal of 
efficiently building high-performing machine learning models. Despite its widespread 
adoption and alleged cost savings, active learning's effectiveness is often hampered 
by annotators' tendency to choose a large number of samples, which hinders the 
learning process. Here, we challenge the conventional wisdom that active learning 
truly reduces labeling costs when compared to strategic selection of samples by 
annotators, whose choices are driven by self-interest in our setting. We examine 
various active learning methods, which are designed to minimize the difference between 
the training and test datasets, with an objective that prioritizes efficiency over 
accuracy. Our findings, based on experiments featuring human annotators and a 
machine learning model, reveal that while they are more cost-effective in terms of 
labeling costs, they are actually less effective than the strategic selection of 
annotators. Moreover, we discover that the choice of active learning method has a 
minimal impact on the performance difference, which is substantial and noticeable. 
These observations lead us to conclude that, in settings where annotators are self-
motivated, active learning's purported cost savings are largely illusory, far 
outweighed by its decreased effectiveness, which is particularly detrimental in 
high-stakes scenarios.  To promote more realistic research on active learning in such 
settings, we urge developers to involve human annotators in a more authentic way, 
with a focus on their actual behavior and costs, rather than relying solely on 
simulations and comparisons to passive learning.

, a well-established solution to the CP problem in nature, has been sought after for decades through various experiments ranging from solar radio bursts to the detection of dark matter. The primary challenge lies in determining the appropriate experimental design to identify the axion, which depends heavily on its properties, including its production mechanism, theoretical framework, and even potentially misleading results from incorrect assumptions about its behavior. This study focuses on the case of solar axion production and aims to highlight the significance of choosing the appropriate time frame for axion detection in space, specifically in relation to the existing data from the HELIOS mission. By considering a production rate that is proportional to $p^2$, a common phenomenon in plasma physics, a new time frame for detection can be determined to minimize potential overlap with other solar axion production processes during the EASIS mission. This approach may also be applicable to other axion production mechanisms in the solar system. This study also introduces the concept of avoiding interference from relativistic particles in space, specifically in relation to the EASIS mission, by considering a production rate that is proportional to $p^2$. However, it's worth noting that the main contribution to false positives from relativistic protons in space can be modeled through particle physics simulations such as Monte Carlo methods. This study employs the LIRiDIA code to simulate a false positive rate of up to 10% in detecting solar axions, which can be minimized with appropriate detection techniques, including the use of multi-directional antennas in the EASIS mission. The development of such techniques is also discussed along with the potential for detecting other axion production processes in the solar system and the effectiveness of coherent radio antennas in this context. This study can serve as a starting point for discussing the design of the EASIS mission with a focus on avoiding interference from relativistic particles in space. The development of anti-coincidence shields and the use of multi-directional antennas, as well as detecting false positives from relativistic protons in space, are also discussed along with the potential for detecting other axion production processes in the solar system. The approach outlined in this study can be applied with accuracy to a year-scale duration of the EASIS space mission, which is being reactivated with the aim to detect solar axions by emitting a beam of photons towards the sun using a linear accelerator. The development of a four-dimensional spectrum of the solar axion spectrum, which can be detected by coherent radio antennas in space, is presented in this research.   neural networks can spontaneously develop patterns of self-consistency in their
  predictions, even in the absence of a corresponding personalization
  objective. This phenomenon is investigated further, revealing that it is
  closely related to known issues with generalization and overfitting. Moreover,
  it is found that these problems can lead to unintended and potentially
  harmful consequences, such as exploiting vulnerabilities in the dataset and
  favoring certain attributes over others. To address this issue, a novel
  approach to personalization is proposed, focused on evaluating and
  constraining self-consistency in the predictions made by the model, with the
  aim of avoiding problematic forms of self-consistency while still allowing
  for diverse and flexible applications. This approach is examined in a
  theoretical context and validated through practical experiments. 

  The concept of self-consistency in predictions refers to the ability of a
  model to generate similar output given repeated input with no change. While
  this property is often unintentionally encoded in models, particularly
  artificial neural networks, it is not necessarily an indicator of a
  well-generalized model. Instead, overfitting and an excessive focus on
  memorizing data can lead to self-consistent predictions that are unlikely
  to occur naturally. For instance, models have been observed to confuse
  individuals with visually similar physical appearances, predicting the same
  output for each. Moreover, self-consistency can be exploited to extract
  vulnerable information from datasets, such as the presence/absence of certain
  attributes. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed to detect,
  constrain, and manage self-consistency in predictions made by models,
  particularly deep ones. This approach involves creating an adversary that
  attempts to discover inconsistent predictions and encourages the model to
  minimize self-consistency while maintaining performance. While theoretically
  sound, this approach is hindered by limitations in accessible datasets and
  the complexity of models. Nevertheless, results from a series of experiments
  reveal that introducing a self-consistency regularization term can lead to
  a reduction in self-consistent predictions with minimal impact on overall
  performance.

It is demonstrated that the exclusion of this event results in a distribution of arrival times that is consistent with a random pattern, whereas including it leads to an overrepresentation of events with known arrival times from the past century. Furthermore, it is found that the cosmic rays exhibiting known arrival times are dispersed over all parts of the sky and among all types of cosmic ray sources as classified by their interaction types and primary forms. Additionally, a statistical analysis is performed to estimate the likelihood of observing such a concentration of known arrival times if the distribution of arrival times is truly random, and it is found that such an overrepresentation is highly unlikely at a 5% confidence threshold. Consequently, it is suggested that there may exist a flow of ultra-high energy cosmic rays that arrive at Earth infrequently, perhaps once a century or less, and whose detection is hindered by their scattered and irregular arrival patterns. It is also proposed that the primary source of such infrequent events might be the Crab Nebula supernova remnant. Data collectors frequently include terms and conditions within their agreements that provide broad access to collected data, enabling them to sell it to third parties or use it for unforeseen purposes.  Our research aims to examine the current state of contractual language regarding data access rights, with a focus on identifying patterns and trends that could potentially lead to undesirable data dissemination practices.  To accomplish this, we developed an automated tool to analyze over one million contracts from various industries across thirteen countries, tracing the history of data access right clauses from 1997 to 2021.  Our findings reveal that, overall, contractors are granted more flexible data access rights than contributors, with the former often given broad access to personal data within the contract itself, although this is countered by the introduction of data anonymization.  Additionally, our research indicates a shift towards standardized contractual language, particularly in areas like e-commerce, with potential implications for unwanted data dissemination.  We also established a publicly accessible database containing our data and analytical insights to facilitate further study and repurposing of our methodology.  Ultimately, our research has the potential to contribute to the enhancement of data protection laws and the creation of more effective anti-tampering measures against malicious data dissemination practices. ological characterization of a specific category of dark matter halos, focusing on their core structure. Research has shown that a vast majority of halos with masses below $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ exhibit a distinct feature of having a compact core exceeding one-third of their total mass. Conversely, massive halos with masses exceeding $5\times 10^{12}M_{\odot}$ tend to have cores amounting to ten percent of their total mass. The intermediate range, between these two, exhibits core structures that are akin to those of the more massive halos. Upon further examination, we identify a clear topological feature - an isolated saddle point existing within the phase space of a specific set of equations describing the evolution of these halos. Moreover, we establish that the appearance of this saddle point is accompanied by an increase in the ratio of the core to total halo mass. We demonstrate that in a vast majority of halos this feature is located within the scope of a specific range of mass scales, thereby providing a topological explanation for the existence of a compact core in these halos. However, we observe that the majority of halos possessing this feature eventually undergo a major merger, thereby resetting the core structure. Consequently, this explanation holds significance only for a relatively short period of one to three billion years.

especially in settings where data is shared without being anonymized. 
However, the current implementation of DP analysis often faces significant 
challenges due to its generally slow performance, making it impractical for 
large-scale data sets and real-time applications. 
This paper addresses these shortcomings by introducing an efficient algorithm 
for privatizing the mean vector of a multi-dimensional data set, 
which is based on a novel modification of the exponential mechanism. 
The proposed method ensures DP under a modified DP privacy model, 
known as DP-for-the-mean (DFM), which is shown to be comparable to 
DP for a single data point in both theory and practice. 
Our results demonstrate that the FKM estimator, a well-established estimator 
for the mean vector, is an optimal solution for privatizing mean estimates 
while minimizing a specific cost function, which is a measure of 
both accuracy and privacy. 
This finding is further illustrated by simulations and real-world applications, 
which show the proposed method to be highly efficient and effective 
in terms of both scalability and privacy, with only a minimal loss in 
accuracy compared to non-privatized estimates. 
For example, on a data set containing 1 million entries, the proposed 
method is found to be up to 10 times more efficient than the 
incremental exponential mechanism, while achieving similar accuracy. 
Our research also yields a suitable privatization approach (DFM) 
along with an efficient algorithm that is ready for use, 
along with all data and implementation details available at $https://github.com/chen199x/dfm$$. 
This includes a Python package named DFM, which is based on the results 
of this paper and can be installed via pip using the command 
$pip install git+https://github.com/chen199x/dfm.git$$. 
The proposed method is suitable for privatizing mean estimates in various 
settings, such as linear regression, clustering, and neural network training, 
as long as the training data is a multi-dimensional data set. 
However, due to space limitations, this paper only provides examples 
for linear regression, k-means clustering, and deep network training. 
The code for all other experiments is available in the supplementary material.

This WSe2 memory device operates differently from another type of memory that uses a vertical p-n junction in Silicon, where it uses an infrared light to switch memory states, but it has the drawback of having zero energy gap at the junction and thus a high error rate, which is especially problematic for its application in quantum information technology. The rising global threat of counterfeit drugs calls for innovative detection solutions, sparking an excitement for nanotechnology-based countermeasures. We evaluate their performance, discuss their applications and challenges, and uncover the most superior sensing materials to combat this issue. Moreover, this comparison is expected to fuel breakthroughs in this field as researchers continue to excel and explore novel approaches.

Abstract: 
Radar cross-section optimization is a critical application in military operations, aimed at minimizing a target's detectability by adjusting its shape or material properties. This problem is highly complex due to the interconnection between electromagnetic field intensity and target geometry, which necessitates a thorough understanding of electromagnetic theory and computational physics. A novel genetic algorithm is presented for solving this problem, combining the benefits of the Nelder-Mead method and genetic algorithms for better convergence speed and precision. The proposed method is demonstrated through two scenarios: optimizing the surface of an aircraft and shaping a cylindrical object, producing results that outperform existing methods. The code used for the analysis is freely available online for download.

Current approaches to risk management in CC platforms are largely outdated and
ineffective, largely due to their failure to consider crucial factors like price
volatility and trading limitations. Furthermore, existing systems for risk
management in these platforms are often slow to respond and lack full
transparency, which can erode user trust. Our proposed solution, a fuzzy
inference system for risk management, aims to mitigate these shortcomings by
utilizing cutting-edge technology and addressing multiple shortcomings of
existing risk management systems in the CC market.

Our approach to risk management in the CC market is centered on a cutting-edge
technology called fuzzy inference, which allows for the rapid processing of
complex trading data, including factors like price volatility and trading
limitations. Our approach also ensures full transparency of the risk management
process, which is critical for maintaining user trust. We have successfully
implemented this approach on the Ethereum blockchain, utilizing a cryptocurrency
called Velas. Our results show that our approach outperforms existing risk
management systems in several key areas, including accuracy and speed.

We believe that our research on risk management in the CC market can be improved
further by incorporating more sophisticated trading strategies, including
machine-learning-based approaches, which minimize costs and maximize profits in
complex trading environments. To facilitate this, we suggest using Velas' native
smart contracts, which provide a secure and efficient platform for developing and
deploying high-performance trading strategies. By leveraging this technology, CC
platforms can provide a safer, more secure, and more trustworthy environment for
users to trade cryptocurrency.  Additionally, we propose integrating Velas' API
with popular machine-learning libraries, which would enable the development of more
complex trading strategies using various data sources, including prices, trading
volumes, and user behavior, which are crucial for predicting price volatility and
trading profits.  With this in mind, we outline the design and implementation of
a novel risk management system, which is an integrated environment for developing,

performance of our risk management system, following the recommended guidelines
for replicability, which was achieved by cross-validating the accuracy of our machine-learning-based strategy and its replication on three separate datasets.  We have made the source code of our risk management system publicly available, which

A common alternative, an efficient method of moments estimator, has been infrequently applied to these models, largely because an expressive finite-dimensional moment condition function is difficult to construct, especially when latent variables follow non-normal distributions.  However, we show that for a general class of linear state-space models, where observations depend directly on the current state, and state transitions are independent and identically distributed, a finite-dimensional moment condition function can be derived explicitly. To facilitate the development of effective contamination control strategies, we must first understand the nature and sources of interference in mega satellite networks. individual across non-overlapping viewpoints, starting from a minimal set of

code is publicly available for download.

  this, we developed an all-face self-supervised training framework that extracts 
  a robust and generalizable representation from a single dataset, surpassing 
  previous Person Re-id techniques. 

  We publicly release our code and results to contribute to the further 
  development of Person Re-id research.

By comparing these approaches, we validate our theoretical findings with actual data. 

  The model we're examining consists of two variables, where one represents the state of the system and the other is a related auxiliary variable; both are impacted by a rough control input as part of the solution to a stochastic optimal control problem. 

  To solve this problem, we developed two separate methods for estimating the value function: a structural method and a nonstructural method based on the Monte-Carlo method; these approaches allow us to compare the results obtained through structural approximation (using finite elements) against those obtained nonstructurally. 

  Our primary objective in employing these methods is to assess the impact of varying levels of roughness in the input data on the solution, with a focus on distinguishing whether changes in the value function can be attributed to the inherent nature of the problem or to the numerical approximation method used. 

  To this end, we implemented and compared both methods, incorporating an expanded set of test cases featuring increasing levels of roughness in the input data, with the state variable being a scalar; both methods were implemented using the FC++ Finite Element library, an open-source, object-oriented library for finite element computations developed by the authors. 

  Based on our findings, we recommend using the Monte-Carlo method as an alternative for structurally approximating a type of stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with a rough control input, due to its superior performance and greater flexibility; this method demonstrates consistent performance across various levels of roughness in the input data, with a notable improvement in accuracy over structural approximation for certain cases. 

  Additionally, both methods employed throughout this study are suitable for multi-threading and have been made part of the FC++ Finite Element library, which is available for download at the mentioned website. 

  As a final note, we reflect on the limitations of our research and explore potential avenues for further investigation. 

  In the appendix, we provide a detailed derivation of the structural approximation scheme used throughout this study, along with a discussion on the requirements and restrictions that need to be met by the finite element method in order to yield a convergent solution.

Our method enables us to identify the instant at which a network transitions from a simple to a complex structure.  We apply this approach to several types of complex networks, including scale-free networks, evolving networks, and hierarchical networks, and find that they develop complex architectures only after a specific period of time has elapsed and a certain degree of degree variation is reached.  We also discover that the condition of having a power-law degree distribution is both sufficient and necessary for a network to be complex in a particular way, but not enough to define the process of its emergence.  Our approach leads to a new theory of the emergence of complex networks, focusing on the dynamics of their degree variation, and this theory is thoroughly tested and validated through multiple simulations and analytical proofs.  Our method and findings are highly versatile and can be adapted to study the emergence of complex networks in various contexts. specific type of binary made up of neutron stars with extremely high spins. Typically, such high-spin events are difficult to study because their distinctive features are masked by the strong signal from the neutron star with the highest spin. However, using the direct-observable method, we can assess the ease with which LIGO and Virgo can detect these events. Our analysis shows that even with significant noise from the most spinning neutron star, LIGO and Virgo can easily detect these systems even at large distances, and the method of detection does not vary much between the two detectors. Additionally, we investigated how accurately these systems' parameters, including the stars' spin, can be recovered from the data after a detection, and our results suggest that with perfect signal recovery, all but the most extreme cases can determine the spin of at least one neutron star. Our findings also reveal that a system with two identical neutron stars, like GW17ai, can be used as a standard candle, and we explore how using such events could aid in determining the density of neutron stars. Furthermore, we address how the extremely high spins of these neutron stars may impact the behavior of gravitational wave signals in the frequency domain, and our analysis suggests that LIGO and Virgo may be underestimating the effect of angular momentum on these systems in their current models. Our study highlights the opportunity to explore the compatibility of observations with theoretical models of neutron stars, and it provides a starting point for further in-depth analyses of specific events. 

This research was conducted using the LIGO Scientific Collaboration's data analysis software, following standard procedures used in the analysis of LIGO and Virgo data, and involving several members of these collaborations. Our study focuses on two specific events: GW200410, a distance-corrected signal with a signal-to-noise ratio of 944 and characteristic features masked by the most spinning neutron star, and GW17ai, a distance-corrected signal with a signal-to-noise ratio of 248 and a mass ratio of nearly zero, indicating two neutron stars with similar masses.

This study introduces a novel, high-DAR environment mapping technique that achieves more realistic lighting effects by dividing the sphere into discrete regions based on the angle between them. Each region is then illuminated independently, with a logarithmic mapping used to accommodate a wider range of light intensities. This approach is particularly beneficial for scenes featuring both distant, intensely bright sources and closely positioned, darker areas, and it also reduces the occurrence of over-bright pixels. Compared to existing methods, this technique demonstrates greater fidelity in recreating real-world lighting conditions, as verified by user evaluation and performance metrics. A few practical applications of this method are also illustrated through scene enhancements and the simulation of realistic, off-axis lighting. This technique is highly versatile and may be applied in conjunction with other advanced rendering techniques, such as dynamic shadows and detailed scene models. Additionally, we have made the source code for this method publicly available. This code, along with instructions and demo videos, can be found at the specified website. We have also contributed a novel environment mapping dataset, comprising a range of artificially created environment maps that incorporate high-DAR lighting effects, to facilitate the evaluation of future research in this area. This dataset is also publicly available online. Our results demonstrate that this technique outperforms existing methods in terms of both subjective and objective performance, as measured by a range of evaluation metrics. This includes a significant improvement in anti-aliasing, with the technique displaying greater robustness in this regard. We have investigated multiple integration strategies for mapping discrete regions back onto the original environment map, with our chosen logarithmic mapping technique proven to handle a wider range of light intensities more effectively. This is illustrated through a series of evaluations, including theoretical analysis and practical application. We have also explored the application of this technique in various scenes, incorporating both artificial and real-world environment maps, to showcase its effectiveness. This technique is displayed in a series of demonstration videos, along with a publicly available code repository containing all necessary integration instructions and examples.
